analysis.one_liner: Requires a state license and registration to buy a handgun and limits purchases to one per month.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first day: introduced March 27, 1995 by Sen. Bill Bradley with one cosponsor, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action was ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national handgun licensing and registration system run through the states: no one could buy a handgun or handgun ammunition without a state-issued license requiring a background check, a safety course, and registration of each gun. It also capped handgun purchases at one per month, cracked down on gun dealers with higher fees, inspections, and theft reporting, created a National Firearms Tracing Center, barred gun sales to people under protective orders, and expanded penalties for gun crimes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by handgun violence would benefit most: the licensing-and-registration system was designed to keep handguns away from prohibited buyers, the one-gun-per-month limit targeted bulk purchases for the illegal market, and a national tracing center plus dealer recordkeeping would help police trace crime guns. Victims of violence committed with guns sold by careless dealers would gain a new right to sue those dealers. People protected by court protective orders would gain a federal bar on their abusers buying guns. States would receive startup grants of up to $200 million to build the licensing and registration systems.

how_it_helps.text: No one could receive a handgun or handgun ammunition without a valid state handgun license, which would require being at least 21, passing a fingerprint-based criminal background check, completing a safety course, and registering each handgun with the state's chief law enforcement officer.

Licensed dealers could sell no more than one handgun to any unlicensed person in a 30-day period, and unlicensed buyers could not buy two or more handguns in 30 days — a limit aimed at bulk purchases that supply illegal street markets.

The bill would have created a National Firearms Tracing Center in the ATF to trace the chain of possession of guns used in crimes, authorized at $20 million per year, and required manufacturers to keep ballistics and serial-number records for handgun barrels.

Dealers would have to report stolen firearms by the close of the next business day, provide security against theft, submit to inspections without a warrant, and face lawsuits from people injured in violent crimes committed with guns they sold knowing the buyer was a felon or a minor.

It would have barred the sale of guns or ammunition to people convicted of violent misdemeanors and to people subject to court protective orders — a category that at the time did not clearly include domestic-abuse restraining orders.
The Attorney General would have made startup grants to every state — up to $200 million total — to build the licensing and registration systems the bill requires.

analysis.who_pays: Lawful handgun buyers would bear new costs and steps: a state license with fees, a two-hour safety course and exam, registration of each handgun, and a one-handgun-per-month limit. Gun dealers and the firearms industry would pay higher license fees ($3,000 per three years, $2,000 per year for destructive-device dealers), security and recordkeeping costs, and increased exposure to lawsuits. Taxpayers would fund the state startup grants (up to $200 million) and the tracing center ($20 million a year). People convicted of violent misdemeanors and anyone under a protective order would lose the legal ability to buy or receive guns or ammunition.

drawbacks.text: The one-handgun-per-month limit and mandatory licensing would have imposed real burdens and fees on lawful, law-abiding buyers — including collectors and people buying for self-protection — not just on traffickers.

Title V would have added mandatory minimum prison terms — at least 5 years for a felon's first illegal possession with a prior violent or drug felony, and 10 to 20 years with two priors, with no possibility of probation or a suspended sentence — a harsh sentencing expansion that critics across the spectrum later came to question.

Dealers could be held liable for all damages from a violent crime 'without regard to fault or proof of defect' if they sold to a felon or minor, which even supporters of gun regulation acknowledged is a heavy standard for small businesses.

The bill would have made it unlawful for an unlicensed person to transport a firearm from one state into another, with narrow exceptions — a major change for hunters, competitors, and people moving, though transport under existing lawful-travel protections (section 926A) remained allowed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On paper this was one of the most comprehensive handgun-control proposals ever introduced: national licensing, registration, one-gun-a-month, tracing, and dealer accountability, with federal money to help states build the systems. The costs are real but mostly fall on buyers, dealers, and taxpayers in the form of fees, paperwork, and compliance, and the mandatory-minimum title is a genuine flaw that an honest supporter would have to defend. The larger problem is that it never got any scrutiny: with no committee hearings, no markups, and no votes, its actual design was never tested or amended, so the country got neither its benefits nor a fair assessment of its costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on its first day and never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Bradley of New Jersey introduced the Handgun Control and Violence Prevention Act of 1995 on March 27, 1995, and spoke about it on the Senate floor the same day.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The referral was the bill's last action of any kind; the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and opponents of national handgun licensing and registration are better off, because the restrictions were never enacted. No one else gained anything from a bill that died without a hearing or a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry and licensing opponents

against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed national handgun licensing and registration during this period, making such bills politically untouchable in the Republican-controlled 104th Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever cast on the bill; the only recorded support was a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, in a Senate newly controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Gun dealers and the firearms retail trade
industries.note: Dealers would have faced $3,000-per-three-year license fees (up from far lower fees), warrantless inspections, mandatory security measures, theft reporting, records demands when traced as crime-gun sources, a ban on gun-show sales away from their licensed premises, and strict liability lawsuits for sales to felons or minors. The industry's interest in selling with minimal oversight ran against the bill's public-safety goal.

Manufacturers would have faced new ballistics and serial-number recordkeeping for handgun barrels, and the bill would have expanded the definition of banned armor-piercing ammunition to certain jacketed handgun bullets, cutting off some product lines. Some manufacturers might have gained from fewer, better-capitalized dealers once new dealer licenses required proving significant unmet demand.

Selling ammunition would have required a federal license for the first time, with handgun ammunition sales conditioned on the buyer showing a state handgun license — a new compliance burden on a previously lightly regulated trade, though the burden fell mainly on sellers, not buyers of rifle and shotgun ammunition.
